items.title: 7.5 Stationary waves on a stretched string

source_refs.note: Topic 7.5 with Fig. 7.7, Example 7.3 and the Brain Teasers (PDF 147-150, printed 144-147). Equation number (7.4) is printed twice, and the text cites Eq. 7.2 for the wave speed, which is Eq. 7.3.

blocks.text: Consider a string of length l which is kept stretched by clamping its ends, so that the tension in the string is F.
(a) String plucked at its middle point

If the string is plucked at its middle point, two transverse waves originate from this point, one moving towards the left end and the other towards the right end. When these waves reach the two clamped ends they are reflected back, giving rise to stationary waves. As the two ends of the string are clamped, no motion takes place there, so nodes are formed at the two ends, and one mode of vibration of the string is as shown in Fig. 7.7(a), with the two ends as nodes and one antinode in between; visually the string seems to vibrate in one loop. As the distance between two consecutive nodes is one half of the wavelength of the waves set up in the string, in this mode the length l of the string is l = lambda1/2, or lambda1 = 2l ... (7.2), where lambda1 is the wavelength of the waves set up in this mode.

The speed v of the waves in the string depends upon the tension F of the string and m, the mass per unit length of the string; it is independent of the point from which the string is plucked: v = sqrt(F/m) ... (7.3). Knowing the speed v and wavelength lambda1, the frequency f1 of the waves is f1 = v/lambda1 = v/2l; substituting the value of v, f1 = (1/2l) sqrt(F/m) ... (7.4). Thus in the first mode of vibration (Fig. 7.7a), waves of frequency f1 only are set up in the given string.

If the same string is plucked from one quarter of its length, stationary waves are again set up, with nodes and antinodes as shown in Fig. 7.7(b); now the string vibrates in two loops. This configuration develops because the string was plucked from the position of an antinode. As the distance between two consecutive nodes is half the wavelength, the length l of the string equals the wavelength of the waves set up in this mode: if lambda2 is their wavelength, l = lambda2/2 + lambda2/2 = 2 (lambda2/2), so lambda2 = l. The wavelength in this case is half that of the first case, and since the speed of the waves depends on the tension and the mass per unit length, independent of the point where the string is plucked, v remains the same in both cases. If f2 is the frequency of vibration in the second mode, f2 = v/lambda2 = v/l; multiplying and dividing by 2, f2 = 2v/2l, and as f1 = v/2l, f2 = 2 f1. Thus when the string vibrates in two loops its frequency becomes double that in one loop.
(c) String plucked at an arbitrary point

Let the string resonate in n loops, with (n + 1) nodes and n antinodes. If the string is made to vibrate in n loops, the frequency of the stationary waves set up on it is fn = n (v/2l), or fn = n f1 ... (7.5), so fn is proportional to n, and the corresponding wavelength is lambda_n = 2l/n ... (7.6), where n = 1, 2, 3, ... As the string vibrates in more loops its frequency f goes on increasing and the wavelength lambda gets correspondingly shorter; however, the product of f and lambda is always equal to v, the speed of the waves.

items: The stationary waves have a discrete set of frequencies f1, 2f1, 3f1, ..., nf1, known as the harmonic series. The lowest characteristic frequency of vibration is the fundamental frequency f1, which corresponds to the first harmonic; the frequency f2 = 2f1 corresponds to the second harmonic, and so on.

In other words, quantum jumps in frequency exist between the resonance frequencies; this is known as the quantization of frequencies: fn = n f1, where n = 1, 2, 3, ... (integral multiples). Stationary waves can be set up on the string only with the frequencies of the harmonic series determined by the tension, length and mass per unit length of the string; waves not in the harmonic series are quickly damped out.

The frequency of a string on a musical instrument can be changed either by varying the tension or by changing the length. For example, the tension in guitar and violin strings is varied by tightening the pegs on the neck of the instrument; once the instrument is tuned, the musicians vary the frequency by moving their fingers along the neck, thereby changing the length of the vibrating portion of the string.

blocks.caption: Stationary waves on strings, in air columns and with microwaves (original diagram after Figures 7.6 to 7.10 and topics 7.4 to 7.7).
blocks.long_description: A string clamped at both ends can only vibrate with nodes at its ends, so it fits a whole number of half wavelengths: one loop gives the fundamental, whose frequency is the wave speed, the root of the tension over the mass per unit length, divided by twice the length, and n loops give n times that frequency. In a pipe the air is free at an open end, an antinode, and held at a closed end, a node; a pipe open at both ends fits whole half wavelengths and gives every harmonic, while a pipe closed at one end fits odd quarter wavelengths and gives only odd harmonics, its fundamental an octave below that of an open pipe of the same length. Microwaves reflected from a metal plate form a standing wave whose nodes and antinodes a probe finds, twice the antinode spacing being the wavelength.

blocks.text: In the above example the set of all the possible standing waves, having frequencies f1, 2f1, 3f1, ..., nf1, are called the harmonics of the system. The lowest or fundamental frequency of all the harmonics is called the fundamental or first harmonic; subsequent frequencies are called the second harmonic, third harmonic, and so on.

blocks.title: Example 7.3
blocks.text: A stationary wave is established in a string which is 120 cm long and fixed at both ends. The string vibrates in four segments at a frequency of 120 Hz. Determine its wavelength and the fundamental frequency. Solution: l = 120 cm = 1.2 m, n = 4, f4 = 120 Hz, f1 = ?, lambda = ?. (i) As the string vibrates in four segments and the distance between two consecutive nodes is lambda/2, l = n (lambda_n/2), so lambda_n = 2l/n, lambda4 = 2 x 1.2/4 = 0.6 m. (ii) If the string vibrates in n loops the frequency of the stationary waves is fn = n f1: f4 = 4 f1, 120 = 4 f1, f1 = 120/4 = 30 Hz.
